newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Big coal expansion seen in Australia's NSW.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Big coal expansion seen in Australia's NSW.

text.p: Australia's Hunter Valley coal province is in the throes of big expansion to meet burgeoning Asian steam coal demand, site inspections of the region show.
A tour of the area was conducted this week as part of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) coal conference at Terrigal, New South Wales.

The conference outlined big expansion plans for coal-fired power generation in Asia and showed important shifts in the the coal marketplace which are likely to break the traditional grip of private Australia-Japan negotiations on pricing terms.

In the New South Wales Hunter Valley, the main coal port and loading facility Port Waratah Coal Services is launching a A$700 million stage three expansion to boost port capacity to 100 million tonnes a year by the turn of the century from existing capacity of 66 million tonnes. This will follow an increase last year from 43 million tonnes, officials said.
An environmental impact statement for a third berth had been lodged with the state government and the go-ahead was hoped for by Christmas for a start of construction next year, they said.
Construction of the new berth would take less than a year but installation of massive shiploading equipment would require a two-year lead time, officials at the facility said.

Finance for the expansion would come from either shareholders -- with the facility owned 70 percent by a collective of the Hunter Valley's mines and 30 percent by Japanese steel mills, trading houses and power utilities -- or from Port Waratah's own borrowings, they said.

The big Warkworth mine -- owned by Peabody Australia 43.75 percent, Nippon Steel Australia 7.5 percent, Mitsubishi Materials Australia 6.0 percent, Mitsubishi Development 22.75 percent and Ticor Ltd 20 percent -- is in the midst of a A$140 million expansion to total production of 4.5 million tonnes a year by 1999.
This will be up from existing production of three million tonnes this year and involves targeted 1997 production of 3.8 million tonnes, company officials said.
All of the expanded production at Warkworth, the single largest coal lease in New South Wales, will be steam coal.
Existing production is a combination of semi-coking and steam coal, with the emphasis on steam coal.

The group is currently developing two new mining areas to bring the total in operation by 1999 to five pits. Expansion also involves upgrading the washery and crushing systems and the ordering of a new US$50.0 million dragline, they said.
Feasibility studies were also underway into opening an underground mining operation, they said.

Delegates to the APEC coal conference said after its close that its key message, apart from the big increase in steam coal demand, was the entry of diverse new players into the trade with US$2.3 trillion in world-wide expansion underway.
The entry of independent power plant operators into the system would begin to open the market to more transparent systems, including futures trading in coal.

Financiers, examining the supply of the huge amounts of private capital required to fund the expansion, said that behind the public talk, smaller projects were going ahead but many bigger projects remained stalled.--Sydney Newsroom 61-2-373-1800
